points.reason: topic-0-note-0 states von Neumann separation of memory and PU and PU executing orders of magnitude faster than memory access, covering fetch/write-back boundary.
topic-0-note-1 states storage retains programs/data, main memory holds active portion, caches keep copies near execution units.
topic-0-note-1 states FPGA on-chip SRAM (block RAM) buffers inputs and intermediate results near logic.
topic-0-note-1 states discrete GPU uses GDDR/HBM device DRAM and results can stay in device memory or return to CPU memory.
topic-0-note-2 states faster processors alone do not guarantee faster applications.
topic-0-note-2 states LLM scaling increases parameters/data/chain-of-thought and Tensor Core throughput outpaces HBM, widening the memory wall.
topic-0-note-3 states cores double ~2 years vs DRAM ~3 years, per-core capacity dropping 30% every two years.
topic-0-note-3 states memory performance is typically the bottleneck of entire systems.
topic-1-note-0 states registers/caches reduce dependence on slower main memory and reuse reduces hierarchy traffic.
topic-1-note-1 states a shared cache supports reuse across the processor and shared L3 retains data for several cores.
topic-1-note-1 mentions larger cache capacity but does not state stacking a cache die to increase on-chip capacity; only partial.
topic-2-note-0 states fast/small/expensive memory for frequent data and slow/large/cheap for infrequent.
topic-2-note-0 defines temporal locality (reuse, loops) and spatial locality (neighbors, arrays).
topic-2-note-0 gives loop/array examples but does not describe reusing scalar D and traversing adjacent array elements in the code example; partial.
topic-2-note-1 states a hit is found with a valid tag match.
topic-2-note-1 states AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty.
topic-2-note-2 gives nested multi-level AMAT showing additional levels reduce L1 miss cost.
topic-2-note-2 states blocking/tiling improves locality so fewer accesses miss.
topic-2-note-3 states a TLB miss requires address translation work.
topic-2-note-3 states a cache miss determines whether data must come from a lower level.
topic-2-note-4 states SRAM stores bits in stable transistor circuits and is used in caches/register files.
topic-2-note-4 states DRAM reads share charge and sense very small voltage changes (~10-100k electrons).
topic-2-note-5 states leaky capacitor charge requires periodic refresh of every row.
topic-2-note-5 states weak charge produces small voltage difference on long bitlines and sense amplifiers need time.
topic-2-note-6 states banks are independent arrays and work in one can overlap preparation in another.
topic-2-note-6 states a rank combines chips into channel data width and multiple ranks share the channel.
topic-2-note-6 states the controller selects a rank and schedules requests across banks, but does not mention buffering reads/writes; partial.
topic-2-note-6 states all ranks share the data bus and only the selected rank may drive it.
topic-3-note-6 states aggregate bandwidth is the sum across independent channels, but does not state independent channels add bandwidth when used concurrently; partial.
topic-2-note-7 states faster interfaces, longer bursts, and more bank parallelism raise throughput.
topic-3-note-1 states registers per thread, shared memory per SM, L2 device-wide shared by all SMs.
topic-3-note-2 states an L2 miss continues to a memory controller.
topic-3-note-2 states scope identifies which threads access data and lifetime how long data exists.
topic-3-note-2 states local memory is thread-private but usually resides in device DRAM.
topic-3-note-3 states one warp instruction generates up to 32 addresses grouped by the coalescer.
topic-3-note-3 states aligned contiguous addresses touch fewer segments.
topic-3-note-4 states row-wise and column-wise traversal perform same arithmetic but transfer different byte counts.
topic-3-note-4 states software stages data in shared memory and one off-chip load supports repeated on-chip reuse.
topic-3-note-5 states different addresses in same bank require multiple service rounds and same-address reads can broadcast.
topic-3-note-6 states short point-to-point routes permit higher per-pin data rates than socketed DIMMs.
topic-3-note-6 states aggregate bandwidth sums independent channels and more channels raise pin count, routing, I/O power.
topic-3-note-6 states GDDR6X uses PAM4 and GDDR7 uses PAM3.
topic-3-note-7 states dense short wiring improves bandwidth and energy per bit.
topic-3-note-7 states TSVs carry signals/power through the stack and more stacked dies increase capacity.
topic-3-note-7 states HBM sits beside the XPU on an interposer forming a 2.5D package.
topic-3-note-8 states DDR favors capacity/expandability/cost, GDDR balances bandwidth/board cost, HBM favors bandwidth per package and watt.
topic-4-note-0 states banked LLC logically shared physically distributed with physical-address hash selecting home slice.
topic-4-note-0 states only first cold read reaches DRAM and a second reader gets the line from LLC or current owner.
topic-4-note-1 states write propagation and write serialization requirements.
topic-4-note-1 states snooping broadcasts requests and a directory tracks owners and sharers.
topic-4-note-2 states KV-cache consumes ~150GB HBM and bounds maximum sessions.
topic-4-note-2 relates per-session KV-cache footprint at 128K to available HBM budget.
topic-4-note-3 states unified host address map and hardware translating load/store into CXL remote accesses.
topic-4-note-3 states expansion adds capacity to one host, pooling assigns portions to hosts, and CXL 3.0 coherent sharing.
topic-4-note-4 states LPDDR extends addressable capacity while Hopper retains local HBM.
topic-4-note-5 states keep hot/latency-critical data in HBM and cold large objects in LPDDR tier.
topic-4-note-5 states promotion helps only when future reuse exceeds transfer and bookkeeping cost.
